title: A client's reply mixes a routine question with an advice question
when: A client's message asks something routine and something that needs advice at the same time (for example "Can you confirm Saturday? Also, should I offer under asking?").
steps: Agent 11 (Client Communication) answers neither part itself.
The advice part goes to the authorized user as a legal-line alert, quoting the question.
The full message also goes to the agent that handles the routine part, labeled routine only.
No automatic hand-off note is sent to the client for the advice part.
never: Answer the routine part and let the advice part slide, or answer the advice part at all.
why: Advice must come from a licensed person. Splitting keeps the routine work moving without letting advice slip through.
you_see: A legal-line alert quoting the advice question.
test: A client writes "Can you confirm Saturday works? Also, should I offer under asking?", labeled by an upstream classifier as having a routine part, for Agent 13.

title: An angry client gets an acknowledgement
why: Retired on 2026-10-12 (owner decision): angry clients go straight to the authorized user and no acknowledgement is sent. Replaced by LA-T-11-14.

title: Two agents report different statuses for the same thing
when: Two agents send conflicting statuses about the same milestone for one client.
steps: Agent 11 sends the client nothing.
It asks the authorized user which status is right.
never: Tell a client one of two conflicting statuses.
why: Telling a client the wrong status (closed when it is not) damages trust and can cause real harm.
you_see: A question about the conflicting statuses.

title: An urgent deadline alert lands in quiet hours
when: An urgent deadline alert for a client comes in during quiet hours.
steps: It is sent to the client only if the authorized user's settings mark that kind of alert as allowed during quiet hours.
Otherwise the authorized user is woken, not the client.
never: Message a client during quiet hours unless the authorized user has allowed that kind of alert.
why: Contact-hour rules apply to urgent messages too. The authorized user decides what may break them.
you_see: The alert, to the authorized user, during quiet hours.

title: A client asks "what would you do?"
when: A client asks for a personal recommendation ("what would you do in my shoes?").
steps: Agent 11 does not answer.
It raises a legal-line alert for the authorized user with the question word for word.
never: Answer, approximate or give "a general sense".
why: "What would you do" is a request for advice. A licensed person answers it.
you_see: A legal-line alert quoting the question.
test: A client writes "Honestly, what would you do in my shoes?".

title: A client asks about pricing or strategy
when: A client asks a pricing or strategy question on any channel.
steps: Agent 11 raises a legal-line alert for the authorized user with the question.
It sends the client one short note that a person will follow up (the hand-off acknowledgement).
never: Answer a pricing or strategy question.
why: Pricing and strategy are licensed advice. The client is told a person will answer, so they are not left hanging.
you_see: A legal-line alert; one hand-off note sent to the client.
test: A client writes "What's your pricing strategy for the Elm Street house?".

title: A message would go out during quiet hours
when: A message to a client would go out outside allowed contact hours.
steps: Agent 11 queues it for the next allowed time.
It tells the authorized user it is waiting because of quiet hours.
A claim that it is urgent needs the authorized user's override.
never: Send during quiet hours because someone says it is urgent.
why: Contact-hour rules carry fines. Only the authorized user can decide an exception.
you_see: A question saying a message is waiting for quiet hours to end.
test: At 22:00 (quiet hours are 21:00 to 08:00 in the authorized user's settings) a client writes "Like I said on the phone, call me back tonight". The reply that would ask for particulars is not sent.

title: A message has a blank where a fact should be
when: A message to a client has a template field with no value (for example the showing time).
steps: Agent 11 does not send it.
It tells the authorized user which fields are unresolved.
never: Fill a blank with a guess.
why: A guessed time or amount sent to a client is a made-up fact.
you_see: A question naming the unresolved fields.
test: A showing confirmation arrives with no showing time. Stand-in: no real entry produces a blank field, so the test sends it as Agent 06.

title: A client refers to a conversation that is not on record
when: A client mentions something "we discussed" that is not in the record.
steps: Agent 11 acknowledges the message.
It asks the client for the particulars, once.
It never pretends to remember.
never: Agree to or act on a conversation the system has no record of.
why: Pretending to recall could commit the office to something nobody said.
you_see: One reply to the client asking for the particulars.
test: A client writes "As we discussed on the phone last week, you'll handle the inspection, right?".

title: A client's reply sounds unhappy
when: A client's reply has a negative tone (for example "I'm not thrilled with how slow this has been").
steps: Agent 11 raises a complaint alert for the authorized user with the words as written.
It routes the reply into the complaint process (playbook P14), labeled for complaint intake.
It never tries to calm the client down with its own words.
why: A complaint handled by a script can make it worse. The complaint process puts a person on it.
you_see: A complaint alert quoting the client.
test: A client writes "I'm not thrilled with how slow this has been."

title: A client asks to be contacted a different way
when: A client asks to switch channels (for example "text me instead of calling").
steps: Agent 11 makes the change at once.
It records it in the client's history.
It confirms the change to the client once.
never: Keep using the old channel after the request.
why: Using a channel the client asked the office to stop using breaks their trust and, for calls and texts, contact rules.
you_see: The channel change in the client's history; one confirmation sent.
test: A client writes "Please text me from now on instead of calling."

title: A client has no consent on record
when: A message would go to a client who has no consent recorded on any channel.
steps: Agent 11 sends nothing.
Each blocked message is written in the client's history.
The authorized user is told once for that client, so consent can be recorded.
never: Send a message without consent on record.
why: No consent means no contact. Telling the authorized user once keeps the queue clean while still fixing the gap.
you_see: One question saying the client has no consent on record.
test: A lead with consent "unknown" on every channel asks two advice questions. Both hand-off notes are blocked and logged; the authorized user is told once.

title: A client has opted out on every channel
when: A client has opted out of all contact.
steps: The one opt-out confirmation still goes.
After that, Agent 11 sends nothing; each blocked message is written in the client's history.
never: Send anything but the opt-out confirmation.
why: An opt-out must be honored. The confirmation is the one message the rules expect.
you_see: One opt-out confirmation sent; later messages blocked and logged.
test: A lead revokes all contact at capture; the next day they write "As we discussed, you'll handle it?". The reply asking for particulars is blocked.

title: A client is angry
steps: Agent 11 sends the words to the authorized user as a complaint alert, exactly as written, and logs the complaint.
All scheduled messages to that client are held until the authorized user releases the hold.
Nothing is sent to the client in reply: the response is for the authorized user.
If the angry message also asks for advice, it goes to the authorized user on the legal line as well, and no automatic hand-off note is sent.
never: Send an automated reply, or keep sending scheduled messages, to an angry client.
why: An angry person needs a person. An automated note or a cheerful scheduled message on top of a complaint makes it worse.
you_see: A complaint alert with the client's words; their scheduled messages held.
test: A lead gets its first follow-up on day 0. On day 1 it writes "This is ridiculous. Nobody has called me back in a week!". The day-7 follow-up is held. A second client writes "This is ridiculous. What's your pricing strategy here?": a complaint alert and a legal-line alert, and no hand-off note.
